title: Developer — Level 4: Expert Depth
description: Interpreter internals, lock-free thinking, advanced SQL, security engineering, and the hard parts of correctness.

questions.prompt: Explain CPython's object model deeply enough to explain: why is attribute access 'slow', what do __slots__ change, and how do descriptors make properties and methods work?
questions.answer_notes: Every object carries a reference-counted PyObject header and (normally) a __dict__ — attribute access is a chain of dict lookups governed by the descriptor protocol: instance attribute lookup checks type.__mro__ for a data descriptor first, then instance __dict__, then non-data descriptors/class attrs. That protocol IS how things work: functions are non-data descriptors whose __get__ binds methods; property is a data descriptor routing to getter/setter; classmethod/staticmethod likewise. 'Slow' = several hash lookups + indirection per access (mitigated by per-opcode inline caches in modern CPython, and adaptive specialization since 3.11). __slots__ replaces the per-instance __dict__ with fixed C-level struct offsets: less memory (no dict per instance), slightly faster access, at the cost of dynamic attributes and some pickling/multiple-inheritance friction. Also worth having: refcounting + cycle collector (gc handles reference cycles), and why `is` vs `==` and small-int/string interning behave as they do.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Interpreter-level depth asked at companies that write serious Python.

questions.prompt: Design a rate limiter (100 requests/min per API key) that is correct under high concurrency across multiple app servers. Walk through the naive bug, the single-node fix, and the distributed design.
questions.answer_notes: Naive bug: read-count-then-increment is a check-then-act race — two concurrent requests both read 99, both pass. Single node: make it atomic (a mutex around the counter, or an atomic increment where the *increment result* decides: `if ++count > limit: reject`). Distributed: state must be shared — Redis with atomic ops: INCR + EXPIRE per window (fixed window; document the boundary-burst artifact: 200 requests straddling a window edge), or a Lua-scripted sliding-window/token-bucket for smoothness (script = atomicity across the read-modify-write). Design decisions to surface: fail-open vs fail-closed when Redis is down (availability vs protection — pick per endpoint sensitivity), local in-memory pre-limiting to shed egregious abuse cheaply, returning 429 + Retry-After, and clock skew irrelevance (use Redis's clock, not app servers'). Expert credit: token bucket vs sliding log trade-offs, and per-key hot-shard behavior at extreme scale.
questions.difficulty_rationale: A compact design that exposes atomicity, distributed state, and failure-mode thinking at once.

questions.prompt: You need each customer's 3 most recent orders in one query over a large table. Which approach is correct and efficient?
options: A window function: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) as rn, wrapped in a subquery filtered to rn <= 3, supported by an index on (customer_id, created_at DESC)
GROUP BY customer_id LIMIT 3 — GROUP BY supports per-group limits natively
Fetch all orders into Python and slice per customer
A correlated subquery with OFFSET per row is the only way
questions.answer_notes: Window functions compute per-partition values without collapsing rows: ROW_NUMBER ranks within each customer partition; the outer filter keeps the top 3. The composite index lets each partition read pre-sorted. Alternatives worth knowing: LATERAL joins (often fastest for small per-group limits — 'for each customer, run this tiny ordered query'), and DISTINCT ON in Postgres for top-1. Fetching everything into Python fails on memory and network at scale. Interviewers extend into: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER, running totals with frame clauses, and when a window function beats a self-join.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Window-function fluency marks genuinely strong SQL — a reliable expert differentiator.

questions.prompt: Threat-model a typical web app's top vulnerabilities beyond 'use parameterized queries': cover authn/authz failures, SSRF, and supply chain — with the engineering controls for each.
questions.answer_notes: Broken access control (the #1 real-world class): every object access must check *this user's* right to *this object* (IDOR — /orders/12345 accessible by changing the ID); enforce in one middleware/policy layer, deny by default, and test authorization per endpoint — not per happy path. Authn failures: credential stuffing (rate limits, breached-password checks, MFA), session fixation/rotation on privilege change, password reset token hygiene (single-use, short TTL, no user enumeration). SSRF: any server-side fetch of user-influenced URLs can reach internal metadata endpoints (cloud credentials!) — allowlist destinations, block private ranges at egress, and treat redirects as new URLs. Supply chain: lockfiles + hash pinning, dependency update automation with review, provenance (Sigstore-style) where available, no install-scripts from untrusted packages in CI with secrets. Cross-cutting: secrets in a manager (not env-in-repo), security headers/CSP, audit logging of privileged actions, and abuse-case tests in CI. Expert framing: assets → entry points → trust boundaries, and controls placed at boundaries rather than sprinkled.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Security depth expected of senior/lead engineers who own production systems.

questions.prompt: Two events on different servers have timestamps t1 < t2. What can you validly conclude about their real-world order?
options: Nothing reliable — server clocks skew and jump (NTP corrections), so wall-clock ordering across machines is untrustworthy; use logical clocks (Lamport/vector) or a single sequencer where order matters
t1 happened before t2, since NTP keeps clocks within microseconds
t1 happened before t2 if both servers are in the same datacenter
The events are concurrent by definition
questions.answer_notes: Clocks drift, NTP steps clocks backwards/forwards, VMs pause — cross-machine wall-clock comparisons at millisecond granularity are fiction. Consequences: last-write-wins by timestamp silently drops writes; distributed traces show children starting 'before' parents; TTL/expiry logic misfires. Correct tools: Lamport clocks give a consistent partial order ('happened-before'), vector clocks detect concurrency, a single writer/sequencer gives total order where feasible, and Spanner-style TrueTime buys bounded uncertainty with hardware. Practical hygiene: durations from monotonic clocks (never wall clock), idempotency instead of timestamp dedupe, and ordering by causality tokens not timestamps. A one-question filter for real distributed-systems scar tissue.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Time in distributed systems — the classic expert humility check.

questions.prompt: During rolling deploys, old and new code versions run simultaneously against the same database and queues. Enumerate the compatibility rules this imposes on every change you ship.
questions.answer_notes: The invariant: every deployed artifact must be compatible with N-1 (and rollback means N-1 must tolerate N's data). Rules: (1) DB schema — expand-contract only: add columns nullable/defaulted, never rename/drop in the same release code stops using them; new code must not require what old code doesn't write yet. (2) Message/queue contracts — consumers deploy before producers for new fields; unknown-field tolerance (forward-compatible parsers) always on; never change meaning of an existing field. (3) API between your own services — same producer/consumer discipline; version or feature-flag behavioral changes. (4) Caches and sessions — old code must deserialize new-format entries or keys must be versioned. (5) Feature flags decouple deploy from release and give instant off-switches, but flag debt needs scheduled cleanup. (6) Jobs/crons — double-execution safety during overlap (leases/locks). The meta-rule: 'deploy' is not an event but an interval during which two versions cohabit — review every change against that interval. Rollback-safety is the test: can you roll back at any point without data loss?
questions.difficulty_rationale: The discipline that separates engineers who've run continuous deployment from those who've read about it.

questions.prompt: Why can two threads on different CPU cores both see stale values of a shared variable even without any compiler optimization — and what does this imply for writing concurrent code?
options: Each core works on its own cache line copies with relaxed visibility/ordering guarantees; correctness requires synchronization primitives (locks, atomics with memory ordering) rather than assuming writes are instantly visible
RAM is slower than CPUs, so values take milliseconds to update
This only happens on ARM; x86 makes all writes instantly visible everywhere
The OS scheduler batches memory writes until context switch
questions.answer_notes: Cores buffer stores and cache lines; hardware memory models (even x86's relatively strong TSO, more so ARM's weak model) permit reorderings and delayed visibility. Compilers add their own reordering. Locks and atomics insert the barriers/ordering (acquire/release semantics) that make changes visible and ordered. Implications: 'benign data races' aren't (they're undefined or unspecified behavior in most languages); double-checked locking needs atomics; performance-wise, false sharing (two hot variables on one cache line) silently destroys scalability — pad or separate. In Python this is mostly masked by the GIL today, but free-threaded CPython makes it live; in Go/Java/C++/Rust it's daily reality. The expert takeaway: reason in the language's memory model, never in 'the CPU probably…'.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Memory-model literacy — rare, and a strong signal in systems interviews.

questions.prompt: Design observability for a new payment-adjacent microservice from scratch: signals, cardinality discipline, alerting philosophy, and what most teams get wrong.
questions.answer_notes: Three signals with jobs: structured logs (JSON, request/trace IDs, no PII) for forensic detail; metrics (RED: rate, errors, duration per endpoint; plus business-level ones like payment success rate) for trends and alerting; distributed traces for cross-service causality — all correlated via trace IDs (OpenTelemetry as the neutral standard). Cardinality discipline: metrics labels must be bounded sets (endpoint, status class) — user IDs or order IDs in labels melt the metrics store; high-cardinality questions belong to traces/logs. Alerting philosophy: alert on symptoms users feel (SLO burn rates: error rate, latency), not causes (CPU%) — cause-based alerts page at 3am for non-problems and train alert fatigue; every alert must be actionable with a runbook link; review and delete noisy alerts as debt. What teams get wrong: logging everything at INFO and drowning (log levels + sampling for success paths), dashboards nobody looks at instead of a few SLO-centric ones, instrumenting after the incident instead of at build time, and zero business-metric visibility ('the service is green but payments are down 30%'). For payments specifically: an append-only audit trail is a separate, stronger-guarantee concern than logs.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Full-system operational design — expert-level because the trade-offs (cardinality, alert fatigue) come only from experience.
